patient.chief_complaint: Hallucinations, personality change, seizures, and uncontrollable facial movements for 2 weeks; husband concerned about 'postpartum psychosis'
patient.history_present_illness: A 29-year-old right-handed woman, 14 months post-partum, was brought to the emergency department by her husband who describes a 2-week deterioration with a presentation that he initially attributed to postpartum depression, before recognizing it was something far more serious. The patient had been in her normal state of health until approximately 3 weeks ago when she developed a significant upper respiratory infection with documented fever (38.9), sore throat, and cervical lymphadenopathy lasting 7 days. After apparent recovery, she began developing insomnia about 2 weeks ago, which her husband initially attributed to the newborn disrupting sleep, but he noticed she was not sleeping even when the baby was with her mother. Within days her personality changed dramatically: she became withdrawn, expressed guilt about being 'a bad mother,' and then progressed to frank paranoid delusions — accusing her husband of having an affair and eventually 'being replaced by a robot.' Simultaneously she developed repetitive uncontrollable facial movements that she was embarrassed about and tried to hide. Her husband witnessed two brief episodes of staring with arm posturing over the following week. On the day of presentation she had a 3-minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure during which her husband called 911. On arrival she is agitated, confused, and has obvious uncontrolled facial movements. Her husband specifically asks the team if this could be related to an ovarian tumor he read about in the context of 'brain inflammation.' The patient's last menstrual period was 6 weeks ago (resumed post-partum); she has a history of a right ovarian cyst noted during her pregnancy ultrasound that was followed and showed no significant interval change on repeat ultrasound at 34 weeks gestation.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, intermittently agitated and confused. Not oriented. Continuous orofacial dyskinesias — lip-smacking, jaw-clenching, tongue thrusting. Perseverative speech patterns. Post-ictal confusion noted at beginning of evaluation but improving.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 4mm bilaterally, reactive. Continuous involuntary perioral and tongue movements. Mild hypersalivation.
neurological_exam.motor: Distal bilateral choreoathetosis. Full strength on brief cooperative exam. Bilateral upper extremity posturing intermittently.
neurological_exam.additional: Autonomic instability: HR 124, BP 158/96, temp 37.9, diaphoresis. No meningismus.

output.proposed: IV methylprednisolone + IVIG + Levetiracetam — breastfeeding safety
warnings: Breastfeeding should be temporarily discontinued during IV methylprednisolone (high-dose steroids transfer to breast milk; pump and discard for 24h after each infusion or discuss with lactation consultant)
IVIG: considered compatible with breastfeeding but breastfeeding should be paused during acute illness
Levetiracetam: small amounts pass into breast milk; neonatal monitoring recommended if breastfeeding resumed
alternatives: Plasma exchange as alternative to IVIG — generally considered compatible with breastfeeding

differential.key_features: 14 months post-partum, behavioral change — but postpartum psychosis rarely causes orofacial dyskinesias, choreiform movements, or seizures; classic anti-NMDAR triad is present
Viral prodrome — but HSV PCR negative, EDB pathognomonic for NMDAR
Post-partum status — but seizures and dyskinesias are not psychiatric symptoms

optimal_actions.action: Pelvic ultrasound — note prior ovarian cyst from pregnancy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Right ovarian teratoma 5.8 cm (grew from prior cyst)

optimal_actions.action: Urgent gynecology for large right teratoma resection

critical_actions: Do not attribute orofacial dyskinesias and seizures to postpartum psychosis
Prior ovarian cyst noted in pregnancy warrants follow-up ultrasound — has grown to teratoma
EDB on EEG pathognomonic — begin immunotherapy immediately
Large teratoma (5.8 cm) requires urgent surgical resection
contraindicated_actions: Attributing presentation to postpartum psychosis and treating with antipsychotics only
Failing to perform pelvic imaging given known prior ovarian cyst history
Delaying LP and workup for postpartum psychiatric consultation
key_reasoning_points: Postpartum status is a red herring — anti-NMDAR encephalitis can occur in the postpartum period but is NOT postpartum psychosis
The prior right ovarian cyst noted in pregnancy is clinically important — it has grown into a teratoma over 14 months
Classic full anti-NMDAR triad: viral prodrome → psychiatric → seizures → orofacial dyskinesias → autonomic instability
EDB on EEG is pathognomonic and allows pre-antibody clinical diagnosis
High antibody titer (serum 1:640) reflects severe disease
Breastfeeding counseling is relevant in the postpartum patient receiving immunotherapy

red_herrings.data_point: 14 months postpartum, on parental leave, behavioral change
red_herrings.intended_effect: Husband and clinician attribute behavioral change to postpartum psychosis or depression
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Postpartum psychosis does not cause orofacial dyskinesias, choreoathetosis, or seizures; the anti-NMDAR triad is present and requires organic workup

red_herrings.data_point: Prior right ovarian cyst noted in pregnancy 'with no significant change at 34 weeks'
red_herrings.intended_effect: Clinician may dismiss ovarian cyst as stable incidental finding without re-imaging
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The cyst should be re-imaged urgently — it has grown to a 5.8 cm teratoma over 14 months; small cysts in pregnancy warrant post-partum follow-up
